units.text: MULTICATEGORIES FROM SYMMETRIC MONOIDAL CATEGORIES
Introduction

This paper aspires to give a thorough study of the underlying multicategories for a symmetric monoidal category. We begin by giving an absurdly large collection of possible underlying multicategories, hopefully encompassing any conceivable candidate for that title. We show that all such possibilities are canonically and coherently isomorphic, so up to coherent isomorphism, there really is only "one" underlying multicategory for a symmetric monoidal category. In particular, any choices of underlying multicategory give a functor from symmetric monoidal categories to multicategories, presuming a reasonable choice of morphisms between symmetric monoidal categories.

We show that a map of underlying multicategories is the same thing as a lax symmetric monoidal functor between symmetric monoidal categories, so the morphisms of symmetric monoidal categories need to be at least lax symmetric monoidal. We also show that the underlying multicategory functor has a left adjoint, assuming we allow strong symmetric monoidal functors between symmetric monoidal categories, since the counit of the adjunction is generally strong symmetric monoidal; it is strict if the symmetric monoidal category is actually permutative. The left adjoint actually lands in permutative categories and strict maps, so the monad of the adjunction gives a "strictification" for general symmetric monoidal categories, since the counit is a homotopy equivalence of categories, although not a categorical equivalence. There is a comparison map, also a homotopy equivalence, to the usual strictification construction due to Isbell [4].

We begin by describing the enormous array of possible underlying multicategories for a symmetric monoidal category, and this relies on the categorical operad Y described in [1] whose algebras are precisely symmetric monoidal categories. The objects of the component category Y (n) can be thought of as a complete parenthesization of a list of length at least n, together with a way of permuting and inserting n variables into slots in the list. The rest of the slots are to be filled with identity elements. There is a unique morphism from any object of Y (n) to any other, so all diagrams in Y (n) commute. Then we will describe an underlying multicategory for a symmetric monoidal category C for each sequence of functions κ n : ObC n → ObY (n) for n ≥ 0, with no further structure. We will write this underlying multicategory as U κ C. The idea is that for each n-tuple x = (x 1 , . . . , x n ) of objects of C, the image κ n x tells us how to combine the objects into a single object using the symmetric monoidal structure of C. Formally, we obtain an object κ n (x)(x) for each x ∈ C n ; we will abbreviate this, and write κ n (x)(x) = κx. For notation, we will always write a morphism set in a multicategory with a semicolon separating the source list from the target object. Then the formal definition of the morphism sets in U κ C is as follows: Definition 1.1. Given an n-tuple x = (x 1 , . . . , x n ) of objects of C and a single object y of C, we define U κ C(x; y) = C(κx, y).
Our first major theorem is then Theorem 1.2. The morphism sets U κ C(x; y) form a multicategory, with objects the objects of C.
The structure is given in Section 2; the verification that the properties of a multicategory are satisfied is somewhat lengthy, and deferred until Section 6.

Our next major theorem shows that these underlying multicategories are all essentially the same. Theorem 1.3. Let λ n : ObC n → ObY (n) be another sequence of functions defining another underlying multicategory U λ C. Then there is a canonical isomorphism of multicategories U κ C → U λ C. Further, given a third sequence ρ n : ObC n → ObY (n), the diagram of canonical isomorphisms
U κ C / / " " ❊ ❊ ❊ ❊ ❊ ❊ ❊ ❊ U λ C | | ② ② ② ② ② ② ② ② U ρ C
commutes, so the isomorphisms are both canonical and coherent.
The proof is in Section 3.

As a result of theorem 1.3, any choice of underlying multicategories for any symmetric monoidal category will give a functor from symmetric monoidal categories to multicategories, as long as the morphisms we choose between symmetric monoidal categories give morphisms of underlying multicategories. This is resolved in the following theorem: Theorem 1.4. Let C and D be symmetric monoidal categories, with arbitrary choices UC and UD of underlying multicategories. Then a map of multicategories (a multifunctor)
UC → UD determines and is determined by a lax symmetric monoidal functor C → D.

The proof is in Section 4. Corollary 1.5. Any category of symmetric monoidal categories, all of whose morphism functors are at least lax symmetric monoidal, supports an underlying multicategory functor from symmetric monoidal categories to multicategories.

Our last major theorem gives this underlying multicategory functor a left adjoint. Theorem 1.6. The forgetful functor from symmetric monoidal categories to multicategories has a left adjoint, as long as we include strong symmetric monoidal functors as maps of symmetric monoidal categories.

The construction is exactly the same as the left adjoint constructed in [3], Theorem 4.2, in the context of permutative categories and strict maps. However, the counit of the adjunction is generally strong rather than strict for a general symmetric monoidal category. The proof is in Section 5, where we also observe the following: Theorem 1.7. The left adjoint from Theorem 1.6 converts multicategories and multifunctors into permutative categories and strict maps, so the monad of the adjunction converts symmetric monoidal categories and lax symmetric monoidal functors into permutative categories and strict maps. The counit of the adjunction is a homotopy equivalence of categories. This is not quite the same as the strictification construction due originally to Isbell [4], and made explicit by May in [5]. We discuss the comparison and differences in Section 5.

Isomorphisms of Underlying Multicategories

We suppose given two arbitrary sequences κ n : ObC n → ObY (n) and λ n : ObC → ObY (n), which determine underlying multicategories U κ C and U λ C. The Relation to Lax Symmetric Monoidal Functors

We have now shown that all of the vast collection of possible underlying multicategories U κ C for C are canonically and coherently isomorphic, so form the target of an underlying multicategory functor that is unique up to unique isomorphism. This still leaves open the issue of what sort of maps of symmetric monoidal categories can be used to give maps of underlying multicategories. This is answered by Theorem 1.4, whose proof occupies this section.

Before starting the proof of the theorem, it will be convenient to make some assumptions about the sequences defining our underlying multicategories. This is justified by the fact that all the underlying multicategories we have defined are canonically and coherently isomorphic, so we can choose any one of them without loss of generality. In particular, throughout this proof, we will assume that both underlying multicategories are defined by sequences of functions that are constant on objects of the same length, so are defined by a sequence of particular objects of Y (n) for each n, which we will call κ n . We ask that κ 0 = 0, the generator in dimension 0 of the objects of Y , that κ 1 = 1, the identity element in Y (1), and that κ 2 = m, the generator in dimension 2 of the objects of Y ; note that the action of Y on any symmetric monoidal category C sends 0 to the unit object e C , and sends m to the monoidal product, so m · (a, b) = a ⊕ b. For larger values of n, we use induction to define κ n = γ(m; κ n−1 , 1).
Note however that κ 1 = γ(m; κ 0 , 1), since γ(m; 0, 1) acts on an object a to produce e C ⊕ a, while κ 1 = 1 acts as the identity.
The effect of our assumed values of the κ n 's is that we are parenthesizing all products by piling up the parentheses to the left.

Given objects x = (x 1 , . . . , x j ) and y = (y 1 , . . . , y n ) of F M, we define the elements of the morphism set F M(x, y) to consist of ordered pairs (f, φ s ), where f : {1, . . . , j} → {1, . . . , n} is a function with no further structure, and for 1 ≤ s ≤ n, f s is a morphism in M( x r f (r)=s ; y s ).
